diaries.speaker: Maya
paragraphs: This is a fictional student diary for the Kanqual demonstration. The voice is synthesized.

I'm Maya. I'm in my second year at Alderbridge. If you had asked me last fall whether I belonged here, I probably would have said yes, because I thought that was the answer I was supposed to give. I had the scholarship and the campus sweatshirt. But I ate lunch looking at my phone so nobody would notice I was sitting alone.

Last week I went to A Seat at the Table, the first-generation lunch. The poster said, come on your own. That sounds small, but it mattered. Usually I assume everyone will arrive with friends. I stood outside Room 104 for a minute, and a student at the door asked whether I wanted to sit with her. She didn't ask me to introduce myself to the whole room.

We talked about office hours. I admitted I used to think you could only go if you were failing. Two other people laughed because they had thought the same thing. It was the first time that not knowing an unwritten rule didn't feel like evidence that admissions had made a mistake.

I saw one of them in the library yesterday. They moved their bag and made space for me before I even asked. That's what belonging feels like to me now. Somebody expects you to be there. You're not starting from zero every time you walk into a room.

It isn't everything. There's a Founders' Evening coming up, and forty-five dollars is my grocery money. I don't own formal clothes, either. I can feel included at lunch and still feel that another part of the university isn't meant for me. Both things are true.

I'm going to the garden welcome day on Sunday. I don't know anything about gardening. The flier says tools are provided, which takes away one thing to worry about. Maybe I'll ask the person from the library to come. I think that's the change. I'm starting to invite people instead of waiting to be invited.

diaries.speaker: Eli
diaries.profile: Fictional 23-year-old third-year commuter with paid work and family responsibilities
paragraphs: This is a fictional student diary for the Kanqual demonstration. The voice is synthesized.

I'm Eli, a third-year student. I commute about forty minutes, and I work at a grocery store four evenings a week. I like my classes. I want to be clear about that. My seminar professor knows my name, and our group project is going well. But being comfortable in a classroom isn't the same as feeling part of the university.

I saw the Stories After Hours poster. Poetry and music, free entry. It sounded like exactly the kind of thing I'd enjoy. Then I looked at the time. Eight until ten at night. My last practical bus connection leaves before it's over, and on Fridays I'm usually closing at work anyway. Free doesn't mean I can get there.

People say, you should get involved. They mean it kindly, mostly. But it starts to sound as though being left out is something I'm choosing. I can't keep explaining my shift schedule every time someone asks why I wasn't at an event.

Yesterday I tried the Between Classes lunch. I only had twenty minutes. Nobody made it strange when I left early. Another commuter told me there's a group chat where people arrange study sessions before their buses. I joined it. So I don't want to say nothing works. That lunch worked because somebody had thought about when we'd actually be here.

The university promotion makes campus look like one big shared living room. I watch that and wonder where the people who leave at three fit into the picture. I don't need to be in an advertisement. I need a place to sit without buying coffee, and plans that don't always start after dinner.

There's a listening session called Make Room next month. I'll be working, but the flier says written comments are welcome. I might leave one. I want to know what happens after the comments, though. If they post a summary and change even one event time, I'll notice. Belonging would mean I don't have to rearrange my whole life just to have a small part in campus life.
